Prior to the establishment of residential schools, Indigenous children often had limited access to formal education. Many were forced to drop out of school to work on their families' reserves or to help with household chores. The residential schools system changed this by providing a structured learning environment where children could receive a quality education and develop essential skills.

One of the most significant benefits of the residential schools system was its ability to promote economic mobility. By providing Indigenous children with an education, they were better equipped to secure high-paying jobs and improve their socio-economic status. This, in turn, allowed them to contribute to the growth and development of their communities.

By teaching Indigenous children European customs and values, they were better able to navigate the dominant culture and participate in mainstream society. This, in turn, helped to break down barriers and promote greater understanding between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians.
